item.title: Lindsay Clancy Murder Trial: Judge Again Pushes Jury to Break Deadlock
item.description:
Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial on Wednesday afternoon again told the judge that they were unable to reach a unanimous decision. The judge then delivered a set of instructions, sometimes called a “dynamite charge,” in a last-ditch effort to push them toward a verdict and avoid a mistrial.It was the second time in two days that the jurors alerted the court that they were struggling to agree on whether Ms. Clancy should be convicted of murdering her three children.

The jury of nine women and three men, who have now been deliberating for nearly 30 hours, were brought into the courtroom just after 2 p.m., uniformly looking grim and stone faced. They appeared to listen to these new instructions with rapt attention.

“You should consider that it is desirable that the case be decided,” Judge William Sullivan said, “and that you have been selected in the same manner and from the same source from which any future jury would be.”

Earlier on Wednesday, a woman accused of intimidation in connection with the trial entered a not guilty plea a day after her arrest outside the courthouse. Her arraignment came moments after the judge in the Clancy case questioned jurors and then sent them back to continue deliberations.

A lawyer for the woman, Dawn Light, 56, said she had been trying to get an image of Ms. Clancy on her phone and did not mean to film jurors. Judge Sullivan questioned jurors briefly under oath before sending them back to the deliberation room.

Ms. Light, who is from Sutton, Mass., was arrested outside the courthouse on Tuesday and charged with “intimidation of a witness, jurors or person furnishing information in connection with criminal proceedings,” according to a statement from Sgt. Gregory Jones, a spokesman for the Massachusetts State Police.

The prosecutor in Ms. Light’s case said during the arraignment that she had been videotaping jurors in a restricted area, in violation of Judge Sullivan’s orders. “The sanctity of the judicial system is at risk” because of Ms. Light’s actions, said the prosecutor, Nicole Piacentini.

Ms. Light’s lawyer, Jennifer White, said she was a retired nurse with no criminal record. The judge overseeing her arraignment, Shelby Smith, denied the prosecution’s request for $50,000 bail but ordered Ms. Light to stay away from the courthouse unless she was appearing in her own case.

In the Clancy courtroom, lawyers from both sides witnessed the judge’s interaction with the jurors, whom he questioned one by one, but public spectators were unable to hear what transpired, and it was unclear exactly what the questioning concerned.

Several jurors shook their heads and clearly answered “no” in response to the judge, who on Tuesday had encouraged them to keep trying to break their impasse and dismissed them at the end of the day with the words, “You’ve come this far.”

Failure to reach a verdict would result in a hung jury, with neither a conviction nor an acquittal. The judge could then declare a mistrial. Prosecutors would decide whether to try Ms. Clancy all over again, in front of a different jury, for first-degree murder or less serious charges. Considering their options could take up to a week, or more.

Kevin Reddington, Ms. Clancy’s lawyer, said on Tuesday that he doesn’t think Ms. Clancy is emotionally prepared to endure another trial but that he would continue to represent her.

When a reporter asked on Tuesday if Ms. Clancy would consider pleading to a less serious charge, like manslaughter, Mr. Reddington said, “Cruz drives the bus,” referring to the county’s district attorney, Timothy Cruz, who brought the original case.

Ms. Clancy, 36, doesn’t deny killing her children with exercise bands in 2023 at their home in Duxbury, Mass., an affluent suburb of Boston. But she has pleaded not guilty, and her lawyers have argued that she should not be held criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Mr. Reddington has said that she tried repeatedly to get help when she began to experience intrusive thoughts after the birth of her third child. But she was overmedicated, he said, and hallucinated a male voice commanding her to kill her children and herself.

Jennifer Sprague, a prosecutor, told jurors that Ms. Clancy had made a series of premeditated choices before killing the children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. Those included asking her husband to leave the house and deciding where and how to kill the children, as well as whom to strangle first.

Ms. Clancy’s husband at the time, Patrick Clancy, said he had found her lying injured in the backyard after the killings. Ms. Clancy had cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window of their home, leaving her partially paralyzed.

The trial has drawn crowds of demonstrators, including many women who see Ms. Clancy’s struggles to get help as an indictment of the health care system’s approach to maternal mental health care.

For a guilty verdict, the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Ms. Clancy both committed the crime and was criminally responsible for it.

Judge Sullivan has instructed jurors that Ms. Clancy would not be criminally responsible if she had a mental disease or defect that prevented her from controlling her actions or from understanding that they were legally or morally wrong.

If jurors find Ms. Clancy guilty, they must choose among first-degree murder, which would send her to prison for life, or less serious charges of second-degree murder and manslaughter, which could carry significant prison time but also leave open the possibility of parole.

If found not guilty by reason of insanity, Ms. Clancy would be sent to a secure psychiatric institution.

Jacey Fortin, Jenna Russell and Remy Tumin contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Administration Begins Blitz to Find Elusive Voter Fraud Ahead of Midterms
item.description:
Hundreds of federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been assigned to an intensive, weekslong hunt for noncitizens among the nation’s registered voters despite an absence of evidence of widespread fraud, according to documents and training videos reviewed by The New York Times.

Agents are scouring voter rolls managed by the states, and are using personally identifiable information about individual voters, such as their dates of birth and partial Social Security numbers, to look them up on those rolls, according to the documents.

In some cases, investigators are effectively posing as individual voters by plugging their names and personal information into public-facing websites run by the top election official in each state. Some of these sites declare they are meant for individual use, potentially raising privacy concerns.

The extraordinary operation reveals the extent to which the Trump administration is searching for evidence of fraud ahead of the November elections. The government is privately calling the effort the Unlawful Voter Initiative and is pulling agents from their normal duties, which include investigating such serious crimes as human trafficking and terrorism.

Given the decades of evidence showing how rare noncitizen voting is, it’s unclear what the administration will discover, how verifiable any findings will be and what President Trump or Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin plans to do with those findings. A database managed by the conservative Heritage Foundation identifies roughly 100 instances of noncitizen voting over a quarter-century. More recently, roughly 400 noncitizens — a tiny fraction of the electorate — voted in New Jersey after a software glitch led to their improper registration.

Mr. Trump has falsely claimed since his defeat in 2020 that fraud is epidemic in U.S. elections. This year, he has focused heavily on noncitizen voting, calling it a “crisis of election security” in a speech in July and regularly making unsubstantiated claims that hundreds of thousands of residents who are not citizens have registered to vote or have cast ballots.

The president has used his claims to justify sweeping voting restrictions that he wants Congress to enact, and others that he is trying to implement with an executive order that remains tied up in federal court. He has also suggested that the restrictions, such as requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote, would help Republicans win elections in what polls suggest is shaping up to be an otherwise unfavorable year for his party.

Mr. Trump’s unrelenting focus on noncitizen voting has concerned election officials from both parties. So far, the administration has been unable to verify his claims, and has effectively admitted at times that its numbers have been overstated. Yet the public repetition of falsehoods about election fraud has continued to sow doubt and distrust in the electoral process ahead of a charged midterm election that will determine control of Congress.

All of it has left voting-rights groups and Democrats increasingly concerned that the president will try to interfere with the election. And it has alarmed former officials with the Department of Homeland Security that the agency is being weaponized as part of the effort.

“This is a nakedly political fishing expedition using questionable methods to intimidate people from exercising their right to vote,” said Amanda Baran, a former senior citizenship and immigration official from the Biden administration.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the department “is committed to ensuring that only U.S. citizens vote in U.S. elections. President Trump and Secretary Mullin have made the integrity and security of our elections a top priority.”

Core to the operation is a compilation of data on hundreds of thousands of voters from across the country. It is not clear if this is the same data the department cited when it announced in July that tens of thousands of noncitizens were registered in four states — a claim that proved to be vastly overstated. It is also not clear what the criteria were for assembling the data: Early examinations revealed that it includes some United States citizens, according to an individual who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the sensitive operation.

Agents have made more than 1,000 referrals to Homeland Security Investigations of cases determined to warrant further review, according to a Department of Homeland Security official. The agents are looking for noncitizens who have registered to vote or actually voted — or for naturalized citizens who registered before they were eligible, according to the documents. The cases then pass to H.S.I. officers who are in the field conducting interviews, said the official, who requested anonymity to discuss internal processes.

According to training documents reviewed by the Times, the agents involved in the operation are part of the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. They received a training video last week, and were assigned voter data to scour from the 50-state list, according to a person familiar with the training.

The documents do not state what agency built the list or where the source data comes from. But a training video viewed by The Times states that most of the initial data came from public voter files obtained from states through various agencies within the government.

The agent’s first step is to see if the voter data is a match to D.H.S. databases that include citizenship information, applications and other data regarding immigration status. Following a match, they are then instructed to scrub department databases for citizenship status and dates of naturalization for a “potential unlawful voter.” This could include noncitizens who have cast ballots, those who have registered but not voted, or those who are now citizens but were registered to vote before becoming eligible, according to the documents.

The agents are instructed to use public voter registration websites hosted by secretaries of state or other top election officials in each state. An internal website for the Unlawful Voter Initiative, screenshots of which were reviewed by The Times, includes links for each state directing agents to these websites, most of which were designed for voters to check their own personal registration status and vote history.

An introductory page on the internal website states that “conducting checks on open-source state voter registration websites” and commercial databases “can offer evidence of voter registration or voting.”

One slide from the training reviewed by The Times includes guidance from the office of the chief counsel at Homeland Security, stating that “it is permissible” for agents “to use these state voter websites for purposes of confirming voter registration status as it pertains to an alien’s eligibility for an immigration benefit.” During the training video, agents are told that the Office of Chief Counsel “has advised that it is perfectly OK” for agents “to use those websites to search records, so those links are there for you.”

During a separate part of the training video, a D.H.S. official gives an example using Alabama’s voter portal.

“I have Alabama up on the screen,” the instructor says. “If you are assigned to cases, Alabama cases, and you want to search their state registration site, you would need the first name, the last name, and the date of birth of the person as it was entered at their registration.”

Some of these public-facing voter look-up sites are intended only for use by the voter. In Florida, the voter status portal includes a disclaimer stating “this website is intended for use by a registered voter to determine his or her voter registration and voting status.” In New York, the portal says, “To use this page, you must be a registered voter in the New York State.” In Virginia, users must check a box attesting: “I certify and affirm that the information provided to access my voter registration is my own or I am expressly authorized by the voter to access this information. I understand that it is unlawful to access the record of any other voter.”

Privacy protections and voter information statutes vary from state to state, so it is unclear what, if any, legal gray area federal investigators might be entering.

Nina Sheridan, a spokeswoman for the California attorney general, said the office is “working vigorously to protect confidential voter data, and we stand ready to guard against attempts by the federal government to circumvent longstanding protections we have in place.” She added that the office will be “monitoring closely.”

The agents from the fraud division who have been pulled from their normal duties for the Unlawful Voter Initiative include a broad range of investigators who specialize in investigating a host of crimes including national security threats and immigration enforcement.

Documents reviewed by The Times reveal that the investigation spans multiple divisions within D.H.S., suggesting a broad, departmentwide operation. While most of the investigatory work is falling to agents within U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the agents are sending referrals to Homeland Security Investigations and sharing data with D.H.S. Election and Integrity, a new division created during this administration and a top priority of Mr. Trump and Mr. Mullin.

Earlier this week, HSI agents were told of a “Criminal Voter Fraud surge initiative” that would start this week, and involve field interviews and “timely prosecutorial review,” according to documents reviewed by The Times. The surge initiative was first reported by CNN.

Yet during training, D.H.S. officials appeared cautious of overzealous investigations and wary of their data. During one of the training videos, Paul Gleason, a D.H.S. official, urged trainees to avoid incorrectly identifying citizens as noncitizen voters. That error has occurred when investigators have identified noncitizens in government records, such as driver’s license data, without digging in to see that they have since been naturalized.

“The purpose of this process is to refer unlawful voters and unlawful registered voters to H.S.I.,” Mr. Gleason said. “You know, it’s not the opposite. We’re not referring confirmed U.S. citizens. So what I mean by that is, is if you believe somebody likely derived citizenship, we should lean towards not making the referral. Right? We don’t want H.S.I. to go to the doors of U.S. citizens and, you know, put them in handcuffs or question them. We’re only referring people that we believe are unlawful voters.”

item.title: Jay Leno’s Classic Car Bill Passes in California Legislature
item.description:
California has the strictest air quality controls in the nation, but with its coast-hugging highways made for convertibles, the state is also known for its classic-car lovers.

Chief among them is Jay Leno, the comedian and former late-night host, who has a garage full of collectible cars in Burbank, Calif., the same city in which he used to tape “The Tonight Show.”

Since last year, Mr. Leno has pushed to exempt classic cars from the state’s stringent emissions rules, and the effort in the California State Capitol has been labeled “Leno’s Law.” But it wasn’t until this week that state lawmakers passed bipartisan legislation that could ease regulations for these older cars.

The bill would exempt some cars made before the model year 1981 from the standard smog checks that determine whether the pollutants they emit are within safe limits. Car collectors say that the current rules in California — which generally require gasoline-powered vehicles from model year 1976 onward to undergo a smog check every two years — are overly restrictive.

“Most of these cars that we’re talking about, they get driven to a car show on a Saturday,” Mr. Leno said. “The car’s parked all day, and then it’s driven home at night.”

The exemption, which applies only to qualifying collector cars, would take effect in January 2028 and be phased in over five years, eventually exempting collector cars made before model year 1986 from smog checks. To qualify, owners must either have collector-car insurance or prove that the vehicle is driven fewer than 1,000 miles per year.

Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, has until Sept. 30 to decide whether he will sign the bill into law. His office said it would not comment on pending legislation.

Democratic lawmakers blocked a similar version of the bill last year. Environmentalists say they worry that relaxing the rules would worsen air pollution and related health impacts like asthma, especially as the Trump administration takes aim at the state’s environmental policies, which are already far more restrictive than in many other states. Various environmental groups have asked Mr. Newsom to veto the proposal.

“Wealthy celebrities like Jay Leno can afford to have their cars repaired to comply with current law and reduce excessive emissions, but poor people cannot afford the costs of asthma and other respiratory diseases caused by air pollution,” said Bill Magavern, the policy director for the Coalition for Clean Air, a statewide advocacy group that has opposed the bill.

Michael Kleeman, a professor specializing in air quality at the University of California, Davis, estimated that some of the older cars covered by the bill could emit about 20 times as much pollution as newer vehicles. Assuming those cars (which are estimated to account for less than 1 percent of the state’s registered vehicles) remain within their mileage limitations, the impact on California’s total motor vehicle emissions is likely to be small, but not zero, said Dr. Kleeman, who is not involved with the bill. The bill, he added, seemed generally out of line with California’s emissions goals.

“Decision makers need to weigh the benefits of honoring our car culture heritage against the public health implications of air pollution, especially since there are so many other efforts to weaken emissions standards,” Dr. Kleeman said.

The emissions from newer cars are usually measured using a scanner that is plugged into the vehicle. But Mr. Leno, who has a large personal collection of historic vehicles, said that it had become difficult to get old cars smog-checked because doing so required an increasingly hard-to-find machine, known as a dynamometer, used only for cars made in or before 1999. The machine works like a heavy-duty treadmill, applying resistance as a car’s wheels spin on its rollers, while a probe inserted into the tailpipe measures chemicals emitted by the exhaust.

“Someone has a car, but there’s no place to get it tested,” Mr. Leno said.

John Kayajian, the owner of a smog and safety inspection business in Burbank, said he was one of a few who still offered smog checks in Los Angeles County using the dynamometer, which is often referred to as a “dyno.”

He said that even though he did not expect the bill, if passed, to significantly affect his overall business, he still felt it was a bad idea.

“There’s some cars that come in here, that while I’m driving it on the dyno, my eyes are burning from how bad the emissions are,” Mr. Kayajian said.

item.title: Postal Service Is Building Ballot Screening System Despite Ongoing Court Fight
item.description:
The U.S. Postal Service has been swiftly developing a complex screening system for mail-in ballots ahead of this year’s midterm elections, despite ongoing legal wranglings over President Trump’s executive order to restrict voting by mail.

The new system, which requires states to tell the Postal Service which voters will be sent ballots so they can be verified before delivery, shows how aggressively the Postal Service is moving to deliver on the president’s directive ahead of the upcoming elections, which could tip the scales of power in Congress.

The agency’s efforts to set up a way to restrict who gets mail ballots, even as the matter is being fought over in the courts, could cause confusion among voters and undermine confidence in the Postal Service as states are close to getting ballots out the door, current and former state officials said. If the new screening system is ultimately put in place, it could jeopardize the ability of people to receive and cast their ballots, they said.

“It impacts not only voters’ ability to vote, but also their faith in a free and fair system that’s equal for all of us who are eligible to vote,” said Kathy Boockvar, a former Democratic secretary of state in Pennsylvania who now consults with officials on election security.

More than two dozen Democratic state attorneys general and voting rights organizations have challenged Mr. Trump’s order in the courts, arguing it violates the Constitution’s provision giving states the responsibility to run elections. Critics have said they fear Mr. Trump may be trying to control the delivery of mail ballots in order to interfere with the midterm elections. Mr. Trump has said the measure is essential to protect the security of elections.

Despite a court order temporarily barring the Postal Service from implementing the president’s plan to restrict mail-in voting, the agency acknowledged on Tuesday that it had continued to develop the portal in case it is permitted to move forward. It asserted that the work is legally permissible, since states have not yet been required to use the portal.

But a whistle-blower said this week that the screening portal is being developed in a rushed and sloppy manner that could jeopardize voting by mail across the country. The Postal Service has disputed that characterization, while acknowledging that it is rapidly running out of time to have the system ready for this year’s midterms.

Twenty states are set to mail ballots to voters by Sept. 19. The first up is North Carolina, where county election boards will begin sending out absentee ballots on Friday.

Jason Tyson, a spokesman for the state’s board of elections, said North Carolina had no current plans to use the new Postal Service portal.

In Wisconsin, where ballots are slated to go out on Sept. 17, a top elections official has said it would be “virtually impossible” for the state to comply with the new Postal Service requirements around mail ballots, according to a new filing in federal court. Election offices, particularly those in rural counties with few staff members, do not have time to manually add the codes that would be required on each envelope under the new rules, the state said.

The Postal Service’s ballot screening plan is a key part of the president’s effort to restrict voting by mail, a practice that most recently has been used more often by Democrats than Republicans. Under the executive order Mr. Trump signed in March, the administration is moving to create state-by-state lists of citizens to help determine voting eligibility and is seeking to require states to submit their voter data to the Postal Service in order to have their mail ballots delivered.

Mr. Trump has publicly said that restricting mail voting could help Republicans retain control of Congress in the upcoming elections. He has also repeatedly promoted false claims of widespread mail-in voting fraud, even as he voted by mail in two elections this year.

According to the whistle-blower, a federal official who filed a report that was shared with Congress, the Postal Service is building a complex system to compile voter data and screen ballot eligibility through a process that is far below the standards of basic software development norms. The whistle-blower said this happened over a period of weeks, instead of the typical timeline of about eight months to a year for such projects.

According to the whistle-blower and court filings, the online portal would work like this: States would upload to the new Postal Service portal a list of the names of voters who will be sent mail ballots, along with their addresses and unique bar codes. States would have to use Postal Service-approved envelopes for all mail ballots designed to make the bar codes scannable.

Once election offices put ballots in the mail for delivery, the Postal Service would screen the ballots before accepting them by scanning the exterior bar code of one ballot in a tranche of as many as 10,000 to make sure that the recipient is included in the list of voters uploaded to the portal.

The agency would reject ballots and not deliver them if the bar code on the exterior of the sample ballot does not match the data in the portal, according to a Postal Service fact sheet. In those cases, the ballots would be returned to election offices, which could correct any errors.

Such a mis-scan could delay the entire bulk mailing, according to the whistle-blower report. Scanning bar codes routinely leads to errors, and the whistle-blower said the new system could be rife with problems because of its rushed development and inadequate testing.

The whistle-blower described a project that was never clearly defined to the developers and lacked written requirements. As a result, requirements for the system often changed from week to week amid ongoing concerns that the system would not be adequately tested, the whistle-blower said. At the beginning of August, software developers were told to have the system ready to go by Sept. 1.

On Tuesday, Representatives Robert Garcia of California and Joseph D. Morelle of New York asked the Postal Service’s inspector general to investigate the new online portal. Mr. Garcia is the top Democrat on the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, and Mr. Morelle is the top Democrat on the House Administration committee.

The Postal Service, where Mr. Trump has been seeking to install his allies in oversight roles, said the system had been in development for months and would soon be available to states that want to learn how it will work. In a statement on Tuesday, the agency said the portal would “provide election officials with a simple, secure, and efficient way to share lists of individuals receiving ballots by mail in their respective states.”

In a July 1 court statement, the Postal Service described a period of training for agency workers and states on how to use the system before it is ready for prime time.

“For states to be ready to use the portal, we need enough time prior to the November 2026 election to train our employees on use of the portal, and to coordinate with mailers,” Steven Monteith, the agency’s chief customer and marketing officer and executive vice president, said in the statement.

But Jonathan Smith, president of the American Postal Workers Union, which represents 200,000 agency workers across the country, said no one in the union had received any training on how to use the new system.

“At this time, to our knowledge, no postal clerk, either in a business mail entry unit or at a post office retail location, has been trained on how they will be expected to accept, validate or reject any election mail consistent with the executive order,” Mr. Smith said in a statement on Wednesday.

A spokeswoman for Oklahoma’s election board said the state had reached out to the Postal Service seeking instructions for how to comply with the new rule, but had not heard back.

Nick Corasaniti and Zach Montague contributed reporting.

item.title: Man Is Rescued From Inside Garbage Truck in San Francisco
item.description:
A man became trapped inside a garbage truck in San Francisco and had to be rescued early on Wednesday, the authorities said.

The man, who was not identified, was taken to a hospital, the San Francisco Fire Department said in a statement. The authorities did not say exactly how the man ended up in the truck, and the extent of his injuries was not clear.

The Fire Department received a call at 4:11 a.m. Wednesday reporting that a person was stuck inside a garbage truck operated by Recology, a private waste and recycling company, said Capt. Mariano Elias, a public information officer for the department.

According to Captain Elias, the driver had just picked up the first load of trash on his route at a commercial address, emptied the dumpster into the truck and compacted the trash once. The driver continued to his next pickup and was about to empty another dumpster into the truck when a passerby flagged him down and reported having heard someone yelling from inside the truck.

“He turned his truck off to listen, and they did hear someone yelling and screaming for help,” Captain Elias said.

The man was unable to get himself out of the garbage truck. Firefighters arrived and determined that the best plan to dislodge him was to dig out the garbage around him. That seemed safer than dumping the entire load, which could add to any injuries he had already sustained.

About 25 firefighters worked in teams to remove the trash. Once enough garbage had been cleared to free the man’s arm, paramedics were sent into the truck to administer an intravenous drip. The goal was to protect him from crush syndrome, a life-threatening condition that can cause tissue injury, organ dysfunction and metabolic abnormalities, Captain Elias said.

Firefighters talked to the man throughout the process and kept him informed. Captain Elias said he heard some screaming and yelling from the man as if he was in pain.

It took about two hours to clear the rubbish and free the man from the truck, Captain Elias said. The man was then taken to a hospital.

One firefighter was injured when a sharp object cut through one of his gloves. He needed stitches and a tetanus shot, Captain Elias said.

Captain Elias said it was not uncommon for people to go into dumpsters searching for food or other items only for the dumpster to be emptied into a garbage truck. He described it as a “high risk, low frequency” call that fire departments across the country encounter. In addition to the danger to the person in the truck, responders also face hazards when dealing with heavy machinery like the truck’s hydraulic compactor.

In 2025, a man died in New York after the dumpster he and another man were sleeping in was emptied into a garbage truck. In 2024, a woman in New Hampshire was critically injured after she fell into a large trash bin that was then dumped into a garbage truck. Also in 2024, a homeless man in Jackson, Miss., survived a similar episode.

item.title: Woman Who Killed Husband Decades Ago Is Sentenced for Killing Wife
item.description:
A California woman who admitted last month that she had killed her wife was sentenced on Wednesday to 36 years to life in prison. More than two decades ago, the woman, Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi, was convicted of killing her husband.

Ms. Olejniczak Marodi, 54, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder on Aug. 5 in San Diego County Superior Court in the stabbing death of her wife, Rebecca Marodi, who was found dead in February 2025.

“The devastating grief of losing your only child to a violent murder is hard to explain,” said Lorena Marodi, the victim’s mother, who added that her devastation ripples into every part of her life. She spoke at the sentencing hearing on Wednesday.

The couple, whose two-year marriage was deteriorating, were in an argument on the evening of Feb. 17, 2025, according to the authorities. Officials said Ms. Olejniczak Marodi stabbed her wife, who was 49 years old and a firefighter for the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection, repeatedly with a knife.

Lorena Marodi discovered her daughter’s body at their home in Ramona, Calif. She said the image still haunts her.

Ms. Olejniczak Marodi fled to Mexico but was arrested last year, according to the authorities. The U.S. Marshals Service took her into custody at the United States border.

The woman she killed, known as Becky to her friends, always lent a hand to animals, loved ones and strangers, said Jennifer Parnes, who befriended the victim more than 10 years ago. One friend recalled how she had revived a hummingbird. Lorena Marodi said her daughter, as a young child, gave away a new white cardigan to a girl who needed it.

“In the darkest moments, it’s been the memories of Becky that kept me moving,” Lorena Marodi said at the sentencing. “It was the privilege of a lifetime to be her mother.”

It was Rebecca Marodi who offered Ms. Parnes a place to sleep for more than a year when Ms. Parnes was separating from her husband, she said. And it was Ms. Marodi who jumped into action if Ms. Parnes’s horses had an emergency late at night, she said.

“The world really lost a good soul on that day,” she said. Ms. Parnes added, “No matter how heavy things were in her world, she always had a way of making people smile and lighting up the room.”

Ms. Olejniczak Marodi had also previously spent time in a prison in California for stabbing another spouse to death.

She pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter in the 2000 death of her then-husband, James Joseph Olejniczak. They had one child together.

A roommate found Mr. Olejniczak, then 26, stabbed to death in Fontana, Calif., in October 2000, according to coverage at the time from The North County Times, a local newspaper.

Ms. Olejniczak Marodi was sentenced in 2004 to 11 years in prison, according to court records. She served her time at the Central California Women’s Facility and she was released to parole supervision on Nov. 20, 2013, said Kyle Buis, a spokesman for the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

Alain Delaquérière contributed research.

item.title: 2 Police Officers Among 7 Shot in Minneapolis
item.description:
At least seven people were shot, one of them fatally, in downtown Minneapolis on Wednesday afternoon, officials said. Two police officers were among the victims, the authorities said.

The focus of a large police response was an apartment building at 15 East Grant Street, about half a block from the Minneapolis Convention Center. The building is in the Loring Park neighborhood on the south side of downtown Minneapolis.

The New York Times

City officials urged people to avoid the area.

Aerial footage broadcast by KARE-TV of Minneapolis and St. Paul showed a large police presence at the intersection where the shooting occurred.

Umecua Agnew, 48, was in the elevator of the apartment building with two other adults and a child when she heard gunshots, she said. As the doors opened, she pressed the button to head back to her apartment on the eighth floor.

“Oh lord, it just felt like the shooting was on every floor,” she said. “I could feel it every time the elevator went up.”

Ms. Agnew, who moved into the building in April, said she stayed in her apartment until police officers escorted her outside. “I just thank God that I was able to get into my apartment,” she said.

Gov. Tim Walz of Minnesota said on X that his “public safety team is responding to a shooting that took place downtown Minneapolis this afternoon.”

“State officials are on the ground to support local law enforcement,” he said, “and we will share more information as it becomes available.”

In September 2025, two men were killed inside the apartment building that was the focus of the police response on Wednesday. In that episode, the authorities said, two men were fatally shot by a third man who “ambushed” them from behind after they got off a second-floor elevator, according to The Minnesota Star Tribune. Both men were shot in the neck.

Minneapolis has been on edge after federal immigration agents shot and killed two protesters, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in separate incidents in January. Scenes of violent unrest and confrontations between protesters and federal agents in the aftermath of those shootings captured national attention.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Madaleine Rubin and Mack Liederman contributed reporting.

item.title: States Sue Over Move to End Federal Funds for Youth Gender Transition Treatment
item.description:
Twenty-one states led by Democrats sued on Wednesday to block a Department of Health and Human Services plan to bar federal payments from Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program for gender-transition medication and surgery to transgender adolescents.

The new rule, announced last month, is set to go into effect in October.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Massachusetts, argues that the new rule oversteps the Trump administration’s authority and fails to justify its restrictions. The suit said the rule violates the law by blocking reimbursements for treatments that some states have determined to be medically necessary.

“We will not stand by as the Trump administration oversteps its authority and twists the facts to justify its bad-faith agenda against transgender Americans,’’ Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, said in a statement. “We will continue to fight to secure access to medically necessary care and protect transgender individuals’ abilities to prosper as their authentic selves.”

The Health and Human Services Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

In a report issued last year, the federal health department said that the risks of gender transition treatments — which include hormone therapies, drugs that block puberty and, in rare cases, surgery — outweigh any benefits. The report prioritized psychotherapy for minors who experience incongruence between their sex and gender identity.

The treatments are already banned in most Republican-led states, and have been the topic of fraught international debate among health authorities. But most major medical societies in the United States, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, continue to support medical gender transition for young people who experience marked distress over their gender identity.

In a statement announcing the rule last month, Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said, “Children deserve our protection, not experimental interventions that pose serious risks and convey no proven benefits.”

The new rule, first proposed last year, is the latest in a series of efforts by the Trump administration to block health providers from offering the treatments to youths in states where they are legal. A previous effort was derailed earlier this year, when a federal judge ruled that the administration could not bar hospitals that provide such treatment from receiving funds for other types of care from the major federal health payment programs on the basis of a declaration by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

According to a recent analysis by the Congressional Budget Office, the government spent about $100 million on gender transition treatments for minors over five years from 2019 through 2023. The analysis found that the rate of gender surgery among minors insured by Medicaid was extremely low, at 3.44 per 100,000 among 15- to 17-year-olds.

According to the lawsuit, the new rule would set an unlawful precedent that the executive branch can replace the judgment of state-licensed medical professionals by prohibiting reimbursement for treatment based on its own criteria.

“No federal agency has the power to directly regulate the practice of medicine — a traditional and congressionally recognized power reserved for the states,’’ Kwame Raoul, the attorney general of Illinois, said in a statement.

item.title: Will the Nepo-Baby Attack Work in the Midterms?
item.description:
Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire is one of the most successful Democrats in the history of her state, a former three-term governor and current three-term senator — and the first woman in any state to hold both jobs.

As the senator’s daughter, Stefany Shaheen, runs for Congress, though, her leading rival is trying to use the family name against her. An ad for Maura Sullivan, a former Marine running against the younger Shaheen in the state’s First District Democratic primary, says voters deserve a “fighter, not a fancy last name,” and accuses Shaheen of acting “entitled.”

The younger Shaheen pushed back in an interview with me this weekend: “I always knew I was going to have to earn every vote in my own right,” she said.

The polls: Sullivan’s attacks might be working. A recent poll from the University of New Hampshire showed her with a narrow lead over Shaheen, who held a double-digit lead over the rest of the crowded field when U.N.H. surveyed voters back in January.

The lay of the land: The race for the open seat is unfolding in a classic purple House district, and it might just be the last messy Democratic primary of a cycle full of them. There’s at least one progressive candidate, Carleigh Beriont, on the march as Shaheen and Sullivan slug it out, but the contest has come to be seen in part as a test of a cranky electorate’s patience with political dynasties.

Historically speaking, New England has tended to like its political family trees. Think of the Adams family — as in John Adams — and the Lodges, a.k.a., Henry Cabot Lodge. Think of the Kennedys.

And it’s not just New England. Congress is chock-full of members related to former members, like Senator Darline Graham, who took the seat of her brother Lindsey Graham, after his death in July.

But nepo babies (and siblings, and cousins) don’t have a perfect record, especially this year. Jack Schlossberg, the Kennedy family scion, lost a bid for Congress in New York (a defeat that followed former Representative Joe Kennedy III’s loss to Senator Ed Markey in Massachusetts in 2020). In the governor’s primary in Maine, the Republican Jonathan Bush (yes, of those Bushes) and Democrat Angus King III, the son of Senator Angus King, both lost their respective contests. A third political descendant in the race, Hannah Pingree, who is the daughter of Representative Chellie Pingree, claimed the Democratic nomination.

But if 2026 has a throw-the-bums out vibe, it hasn’t dissuaded other candidates with distinguished political lineage from running this year, either. They include:

John E. Sununu, 61, the former senator running for Senate, who is both the son and brother of former New Hampshire governors and is expected to cruise to victory over former Senator Scott Brown next Tuesday in the Republican primary.

Representative Tom Kean, Jr., 57, a Republican, is running for re-election to his New Jersey House seat after an absence from Congress that he ascribed to depression. He featured his father, Gov. Tom Kean, in a new ad.

Beau Bayh, 30, the son of former Indiana senator (and governor) Evan Bayh, is the Democratic nominee for secretary of state.

Michael Alfonso, 26, the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is the Republican nominee for the solidly red congressional district in Wisconsin that Duffy once held.

I caught up with Stefany Shaheen this past weekend at a low-key fund-raiser in the gently sloping backyard of Alderman Jason Bonilla of Manchester.

Shaheen has tread carefully around her family ties in an anti-establishment year. Last fall, she sharply criticized the deal that her mother the senator helped negotiate to end the government shutdown, seizing on Democratic anger across the country.

Shaheen, who served one term as a city councilor in Portsmouth and was chair of the police commission there, has focused her race on health care, proclaiming support for Medicare for All. She told the crowd in Manchester that she was running because of her opposition to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — another person who, as it happens, had a parent in the Senate.

On Saturday, she emphasized her deep roots in the state — “I’ve been here my whole life,” she said, drawing an implicit contrast with the more recently arrived Sullivan — but, on the stump, she used her father’s family history to illustrate that point, rather than her mother’s.

Shaheen has tried to turn Sullivan’s denunciations back on her. “I think the attempt to, you know, attack or target me is a way to distract people from who’s behind her campaign,” she said. Shaheen has repeatedly criticized Sullivan for accepting about $300,000 from people who have also given to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, including in an attack ad that began airing last month.

“Maura isn’t endorsed by AIPAC, and she hasn’t taken a dime from AIPAC or any corporate PAC,” Natalie Silver, Sullivan’s campaign manager, said.

Sullivan moved to New Hampshire shortly before announcing her first run for Congress in 2017. She lost the primary the following year to Chris Pappas, a darling of the state’s political establishment whose run for the Senate has opened the seat.

“Voters have a choice in this election,” Sullivan wrote on social media this week. “Change or more of the same.”

In One Graphic

President Trump’s plans to remake Washington extend far beyond the White House ballroom, where construction was approved to continue Monday by the Supreme Court.

The six ongoing or planned construction projects the president has his sights on are supposed to be scrutinized by independent boards and commissions, whose job is to safeguard Washington’s monumental core. Trump has stacked those boards with allies, leaving opponents of the projects to turn to the courts — a route that can be difficult, as the Supreme Court ruling showed.

NUMBER OF THE DAY

That’s the margin by which Senator Ed Markey, 80, beat his much younger opponent, Representative Seth Moulton, 47, to cruise to victory in Tuesday night’s Democratic primary for Senate in Massachusetts. Read more about the generational upset that wasn’t here.

ONE LAST THING

The ’90s navigation pioneer MapQuest refused to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America on its interface after President Trump ordered the change as part of his trade war with Canada.

Now, it is enjoying a boost in downloads. (It kept the Gulf of Mexico, too.)

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

item.title: Judge Blocks Trump’s Second Try to Restrict Birthright Citizenship
item.description:
A federal judge in Maryland temporarily blocked much of President Trump’s latest effort to withhold citizenship from babies born in the United States to noncitizen parents.

The judge ruled that the Supreme Court had already settled questions reopened by an executive order Mr. Trump signed in August.

While the decision was limited to children born after Feb. 19, 2025, including those born in the future, Judge Deborah L. Boardman wrote that the order would likely affect babies the Supreme Court had already defined as citizens. The ruling delivered a sharp rejection of the president’s renewed efforts to restrict birthright citizenship, after the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in July that a previous, more sweeping executive order from 2025 was unconstitutional.

“No presidential executive order can undo what the Supreme Court has done,” she wrote.

Judge Boardman’s order took a dim view of the Trump administration’s reasoning, which she characterized as a thinly veiled attempt to get around the Supreme Court’s decision. She wrote that the president and others named in the lawsuit “completely misread” the majority’s opinion and embraced a “distorted interpretation” of its conclusions.

In a 35-page opinion, she described the latest order as only the most recent attempt to curtail birthright citizenship by any means that could survive legal scrutiny.

“Since his second term in office began on January 20, 2025, the president has tried, through executive order, to upend our country’s longstanding tradition of birthright citizenship and eliminate, for large swaths of Americans, the right to citizenship by birth, a right enshrined in the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment,” she wrote.

Judge Boardman described a number of ways that children covered by the lawsuit could have their citizenship rescinded, including if the Trump administration moved to label their parents members of terrorist groups or “alien enemies” under arbitrary legal determinations. She cited a pattern in which the administration has accused Venezuelan nationals of being affiliated with the criminal organization Tren de Aragua, often without evidence, in deportation proceedings.

While she stressed that it was too soon to find that the order itself was unconstitutional, she wrote that it already appeared clear that it was unconstitutional as applied to the class of babies defined when immigration groups initially sued last year to block Mr. Trump’s first order.

The order this year had included other measures to create novel categories of babies that could be disqualified from citizenship, including those born to parents engaged in so-called “birth tourism,” through which mothers deliberately traveled to the United States to give birth.

It was unclear how the Trump administration planned to tag those it suspected of traveling to the United States to have their children. But Judge Boardman noted that the executive order was broad, describing anyone who engaged in a “commercial transaction” — such as purchasing a plane ticket — as traveling to access birthright citizenship.

The Supreme Court’s decision upholding birthright citizenship “is the law of the land,” Judge Boardman wrote. “The president must follow it.”

item.title: As Midterms Loom, Democrats Feud Over Defections
item.description:
A single vote on a routine measure that will never become law has touched off a firestorm of recriminations among House Democrats on Capitol Hill, offering a glimpse of simmering tensions within the party weeks before midterm elections in which they are pressing to win control of Congress.

The drama began Tuesday afternoon, when two of the most conservative Democrats in the House broke with their party to pave the way for votes on a slate of Republican bills.

By Wednesday, it had mushroomed into a full-on furor featuring accusations of betrayal, demands for punishment for the defectors and a quiet but intense round of whispers about what the episode said about the leadership of Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, who is in line to be speaker should his party win the majority in November.

Mr. Jeffries said he had been blindsided by the decision by the two lawmakers, Representatives Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, to side with Republicans on a procedural measure, and suggested that it had been the job of the chief vote-counter and No. 2 Democrat to be aware of such things.

“You’ll have to talk to Katherine,” he told reporters after the vote on Tuesday, referring to Representative Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts. (Ms. Clark later said that she had not been apprised.)

Top Democrats demanded that the renegades be disciplined for straying from the party line.

“I think there should be a punishment,” said Representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee. “I think there should be consequences.”

Facing an outcry from their members, House Democratic leaders said in a sharp statement on Tuesday night that Mr. Golden and Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez had committed a “significant breach of trust” that required “a serious response.”

Still, by Wednesday evening, no such action had come. Mr. Jeffries said that members were still debating whether and how to discipline Mr. Golden, who is leaving office at the end of the year, and Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez, who is running for re-election in a competitive district.

“We haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out,” he told reporters.

But Democrats, including some of the most senior in the party, continued to seethe.

Among the legislation that advanced to the floor under the measure they supported was a bill condemning socialism and calling for an election security crackdown, part of an effort by Republicans to paint Democrats as radical, tie them to left-wing figures who are unpopular in swing districts and hurt them at the polls.

“In a week when we should be talking about affordability, because of their votes we have to talk about bullshit stuff like socialism and, you know, all these other nonbinding resolutions that mean nothing,” said Representative Jim McGovern of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Rules Committee.

Nearly all Democrats voted on Tuesday against Republicans’ anti-socialism resolution, in part because of the election restriction provisions that many of them viewed as unacceptable moves to suppress voting.

In a blunt sign of his anger, Mr. McGovern turned his back on Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez as she spoke on Wednesday at a Rules Committee hearing.

The infighting suggested a split among Democratic leaders, raising eyebrows among lawmakers. It also suggested that Mr. Jeffries, should he win the gavel next year, might suffer the very same difficulties that have plagued Speaker Mike Johnson as he has struggled to corral his fractious and razor-thin Republican majority.

To bring most bills to the floor, House leaders must pass procedural measures known as “rules” that do not have the force of law but are necessary to move legislation to a final vote. They are typically approved on party-line votes in which all members of the majority are in favor, whether they back the legislation or not. Members in the minority, in turn, reflexively oppose rules, regardless of their position on the underlying bill.

But in recent years, a group of far-right Republicans, unhappy with their leaders, has repeatedly refused to back such measures. House Democrats, shut out of decision-making in a body where the majority rules, have generally declined to step in and ease their path by voting in favor of rules, consistently sticking together and forcing Republicans to resolve their internal disputes or abandon their agenda.

On Tuesday, however, as a handful of Republicans voted against a rule needed to bring up several bills, appearing to doom it to defeat, Mr. Golden and Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez violated the long-held precedent and stepped in to cast the deciding votes in favor, allowing the measure to pass and bucking the unity that had been a point of pride for Democrats.

Both of them said they were motivated to break from their party in order to ensure a vote on a bill co-sponsored by Mr. Golden that would help lobstermen in Maine by delaying the implementation of regulations meant to protect whales.

But some Democrats said they were concerned that the move might presage future breaks should the party win the majority.

Mr. McGovern said he wanted to ensure that Democrats would avoid the messy battles that had so threatened Republicans’ control of the chamber that they have been at times forced to cancel votes.

“What I want to make sure is that we don’t become them,” Mr. McGovern said of Republicans. “If we’re in charge, people expect us to do things, get things to the floor, move legislation. I mean, they can’t.”

Representative Chrissy Houlahan of Pennsylvania said the defections were “a big wake-up call for people to understand that it’s likely that we’ll be in the majority, and that we need to be a lot more tightly under control.”

In their joint statement, Democratic leaders said they had referred the matter to a party committee that governs caucus rules. But that group is not responsible for disciplining members, and though the matter was discussed on Wednesday at a previously scheduled meeting it held, Ms. Clark said that leaders needed to have “a discussion with the broader caucus.”

Representative Mike Levin, Democrat of California and the head of that panel, told reporters that members made “a variety of suggestions to change our rules” but that any such changes were not going to be immediate.

Any move to punish Mr. Golden or Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez would need to come from Democratic leaders. The most common disciplinary tools have been to strip members of their committee assignments or deny them coveted spots in the next Congress.

Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez’s lone committee seat is on the powerful Appropriations Committee, which controls spending. But she dismissed concerns about being taken off the panel, and in her rural, Republican-leaning district, a high-profile feud with party leaders could potentially strengthen her re-election bid.

“If that’s what they feel they need to do, it’s not going to change how I represent my district,” Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez said, adding that she “slept like a baby” on Tuesday night.

Still, her decision may have political consequences for others in her party who cast their votes against the measure condemning socialism.

Eight Democrats, including Mr. Golden and Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez, most of them in battleground or right-leaning districts, crossed party lines to vote with Republicans on the bill, inflaming a fight that has consumed the party this year over insurgent, left-leaning candidates.

Darializa Avila Chevalier, a democratic socialist who defeated a five-term congressman and top Jeffries ally in a primary in New York, condemned the vote and attacked the defectors.

“Democrats love talking about a ‘big tent,’ but then they vote in line with Republicans hellbent on destroying our democracy and stripping Black and brown people of the right to vote,” Ms. Chevalier said in a statement.

Olivia Diaz contributed reporting.

item.title: El-Sayed Wants to Mend Ties With Jewish Democrats, but Some Are Not Impressed
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, recently spent two days trying to mend fences with Jewish Democrats after an acrimonious primary against a pro-Israel opponent.

For some of them, it wasn’t enough.

Specifically, Dr. El-Sayed sought to address remarks he had made shortly after an attack on a synagogue in the Detroit area in March that some interpreted as too sympathetic to the assailant. But his apologies last weekend fell short with some Jewish Democrats in part because he seemed to be seeking forgiveness for the timing of his remark rather than its substance.

Dr. El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel has concerned many Jewish Democrats. And some are angered by his association with Hasan Piker, a provocative streamer whose comments about Israel have drawn blowback from Democrats and Republicans.

The frictions revealed the still-fresh wounds from a bitter primary struggle between Dr. El-Sayed and his pro-Israel opponent, Representative Haley Stevens. Their race became a proxy war over the Democratic Party’s divisions on Israel, which propelled numerous progressive candidates, including Dr. El-Sayed, to victory.

The lingering tension is a hurdle for Dr. El-Sayed as he seeks to turn to his general-election opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican. Uniting Democrats is proving difficult for Dr. El-Sayed, who won his primary by fewer than 18,000 votes. And he is battling on two fronts, as Mr. Rogers and other Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have begun to assail him over his position on Israel in an effort to peel off Jewish support.

With just over two months left before the general election, the dissonance could threaten Dr. El-Sayed’s efforts to assemble a winning coalition in a key Senate battleground race that will help determine control of the upper chamber.

Dr. El-Sayed is “under a microscope in the Jewish community,” said Yifat Clein, 41, an Israeli-American from Detroit who is supporting him. She said she was concerned about the number of Jewish Democrats in her community who have said they would vote for Mr. Rogers, because of his support for Israel.

Zach Nessel, the secretary of the Michigan Jewish Democratic Caucus, the organization that Dr. El-Sayed addressed twice over the weekend, said that Dr. El-Sayed’s “apology didn’t go far enough.” Mr. Nessel, who is the son of state Attorney General Dana Nessel, added, “I don’t think Abdul has done enough at this point in time to gain our full support with an endorsement.”

Dr. El-Sayed has been meeting with Jewish leaders in Michigan and expanding his outreach, including hiring a Jewish liaison, his campaign said. He will “continue to be actively engaged with those communities to build the coalition that will defeat Rogers,” Cole Wozniak, a spokesman for Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign, said in a statement.

Back in March, Dr. El-Sayed angered many Jewish Michiganders when he described how the assailant at a synagogue in West Bloomfield Township, a U.S. citizen of Lebanese descent, had lost his family in an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon a week earlier.

“Hurt people hurt people,” Dr. El-Sayed said then, while also denouncing antisemitism and condemning the actions of the perpetrator, who drove a vehicle into a building full of preschoolers, injuring a guard before he was killed in a firefight.

On Saturday, Dr. El-Sayed apologized for those remarks during an appearance before the Jewish Democratic Caucus at a party convention in Lansing. He did so again at the caucus’s private fund-raising gathering on Sunday.

“There’s opportunity for context later on, but when you give the wrong — the right medicine at the wrong time, it’s the wrong medicine,” Dr. El-Sayed said at the fund-raiser on Sunday, according to audio provided by his campaign. “And I gave it at the wrong time, and folks didn’t need to hear it, didn’t want to hear it. It was not the right thing to say.”

As Mr. Nessel saw it, Dr. El-Sayed had “apologized for when he said what he said, but not what he said.”

Decky Alexander, the chair of the Michigan Jewish Democratic Caucus, a subgroup of the state party, said the meetings had helped ease tensions for some, and gave voice to “the differing perspectives of those who are Jews and Democrats in Michigan.” She did not say whether the group would endorse Dr. El-Sayed.

Jewish voters have overwhelmingly supported Democratic candidates in recent elections. But some Jewish leaders said that Dr. El-Sayed’s views could mean that he might underperform. He has been a vocal critic of Israel, calling the country’s government “evil” and its actions in Gaza a “genocide.” He also sharply criticized a major pro-Israel super PAC that spent millions in the primary trying to boost Ms. Stevens.

Some say they are breaking ranks with their party to back Mr. Rogers, who has wasted no time courting some of the state’s roughly 130,000 Jewish residents. He campaigned with a prominent rabbi from Ann Arbor last week and has circulated a list of 344 Jewish residents in Michigan, some of them Democrats, who have pledged to support his campaign.

Stacey Gittleman, 57, a Democrat who is voting for Mr. Rogers and signed a public letter urging others to do so, said Dr. El-Sayed’s apology was insufficient and voiced concerns about growing criticism of Israel in the Democratic Party.

“Now we don’t see ourselves as valued partners in the direction that the Democratic Party is going unless we check our Zionism and support for Israel at the door,” she said.

Dr. El-Sayed’s posture toward Mr. Piker, who campaigned with him in the primary and has faced criticism for recent comments suggesting Jewish Americans could face threats over their positions on Israel, has also drawn scrutiny. Mr. Rogers has sought to make his opponent’s ties to Mr. Piker a liability, calling him Dr. El-Sayed’s “running mate.”

Dr. El-Sayed distanced himself from Mr. Piker’s remarks, saying “Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence,” and that he does not have any intention to campaign with Mr. Piker in the general election. But he has stopped short of denouncing Mr. Piker directly, as some Jewish Democrats have demanded.

“This is not a campaign that is about a Twitch streamer in California. This is about affordability in Michigan,” Dr. El-Sayed told reporters on Saturday.

In an interview last week, Mr. Piker called the G.O.P. efforts a “smear campaign” and said it was Dr. El-Sayed’s opposition to U.S. aid for Israel, not his association with Mr. Piker, that had put a target on his back.

Andy Ross, a Jewish Democratic Caucus member and volunteer who helps run the “Jews for Abdul” Facebook page, predicted that the majority of Jewish voters would support Dr. El-Sayed regardless of his views on Israel.

“He’s not Jewish, and he’s not going to say everything that some of those folks want to hear,” said Mr. Ross. “But what I think that he did is addressed those who are open-minded and fair-minded, and willing to consider him.”

Stacie Chaiken of Detroit, a Jewish voter who supports Dr. El-Sayed, said Dr. El-Sayed may face bias because of his Arab heritage and Muslim faith. His comments after the synagogue attack were “misinterpreted” by some as justification for the incident, she argued, and “maligned” by those already “inclined to distrust him.”

“There are some people, when your name is Abdulrahman El-Sayed, it will never help,” she said, adding, “It’s a shame that the Jewish community is so torn apart by things that are happening abroad, and that there is so much deep fear.”

Michigan has been at the center of tensions over the Israel-Gaza war. Muslim voters and progressive Democrats led a campaign to vote “uncommitted” in protest of then-President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s support for Israel in the 2024 Democratic primary.

At a rally in the Detroit suburbs on Monday, Vice President JD Vance met with the rabbi of Temple Israel, the synagogue that was attacked, as well as the guard who was injured there.

Calling Dr. El-Sayed “very, very evil,” Mr. Vance said voters had a chance to “reject” the “hatred” he said is on the rise in the U.S. by electing Mr. Rogers.

Rabbi Asher Lopatin, who campaigned for Mr. Rogers last week, says he has voted for Democrats his entire life. While Mr. Rogers still “has a lot of work to do also to reach out to the Jewish community and to address concerns,” he said, he feels he is the best option.

“There are many things that he’ll probably vote for that I would disagree with, but I think for the long term of the Democratic Party and for the country, we need to defeat El-Sayed,” Rabbi Lopatin said.

Ms. Clein said she felt Dr. El-Sayed’s “questioning” of the Israeli government was warranted and “necessary.” She is concerned that pro-Israel Democrats backing Mr. Rogers would help elevate a candidate who does not reflect their values on other issues.

“You’re not necessarily in love with the person that you’re voting for, right?” said Ms. Clein. “You have to be more strategic.”

item.title: White House Plans $250,000 Renovation of 2-Lane Bowling Alley
item.description:
President Trump’s affinity for golf is well known. So is his baseball and football fandom.

But bowling?

A $253,000 government contract funded by the Executive Office of the President was awarded for a “lighting project” on the two-lane bowling alley in the basement of the White House’s Eisenhower Executive Office Building, according to federal procurement data.

Mr. Trump has not spoken, at least publicly, about an interest in bowling, and a White House spokesman said that Mr. Trump was not involved in the project. But the president has directed makeovers in and around the White House totaling hundreds of millions in taxpayer expenses, including attempts to beautify the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a paved-over Rose Garden and the sprawling White House ballroom project.

The spokesman said the bowling alley project would cover standard upkeep and fixing broken lights, and added that the alley had hosted nearly 10,000 guests over the last year.

Charles Mann Enterprises, the Washington-based construction management firm contracted for the project, did not respond to requests for comment.

Its founder, Charles Mann, is a three-time Super Bowl champion who played a decade for the Washington Redskins. The firm has received at least $3 million in recent federal contracts for work that has included fixing a roof and an air-conditioning system.

An additional $878,000 contract was awarded to Charles Mann Enterprises for a “studio project” in the same basement as the bowling alley. Details on the projects were not available in federal procurement records.

A rebuild of the aging bowling lanes was proposed in 2014 under President Barack Obama. But the project was swiftly nixed after Republicans criticized any use of public funding for the exclusive lanes.

The two-lane bowling alley was first installed in the White House’s basement in 1947 during the sport’s midcentury boom. The project was paid for by a group of Missourians as a 63rd birthday present to President Harry S. Truman. A White House staff member said at the time he was perplexed by the gift, given that Mr. Truman had not bowled since he was a teenager. President Dwight D. Eisenhower moved the alley in 1955 to the Eisenhower Executive Office Building.

President Richard M. Nixon, an avid bowler, built a separate one-lane bowling alley underneath the White House in 1973. President Trump renovated that alley in 2019.

item.title: D.S.A. Chapter Endorses Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles
item.description:
The Democratic Socialists of America’s Los Angeles chapter announced on Wednesday that it had endorsed Nithya Raman, the progressive City Council member challenging Mayor Karen Bass in this year’s election.

The decision came after weeks of heated debate within the chapter. Some had argued that Ms. Raman, herself a member of the group, had recently distanced herself from the organization and broken with it on key issues. Still, more than 60 percent of voting members opted to support her with an endorsement, said Sean Wakasa, co-chair of the Los Angeles D.S.A. chapter.

“We have thousands of members who are ready to organize, talk to their neighbors, knock on doors and build power to shake up Los Angeles and build a brighter future,” Mr. Wakasa said.

Democratic socialists have risen to power in New York, Seattle and other cities around the country, but it was uncertain exactly how the Los Angeles endorsement might land with the city’s voters.

In a city known as a bastion of left-leaning politics, Ms. Raman was the first D.S.A. member elected to the Los Angeles City Council in 2020, when she unseated an incumbent. She is now facing Ms. Bass, who is seen as a more mainstream Democrat, trying to win over a range of voters in a city where moderates, homeowners and labor groups have long wielded significant power.

On Wednesday, Ms. Raman responded to the endorsement by thanking the group for “joining our broad coalition of Angelenos.”

She added that her campaign “is bringing together people who may not agree on every issue but share a commitment to making Los Angeles work better.”

Asked about the endorsement, Ms. Bass’s campaign drew attention to positions Ms. Raman has taken, pointing to her opposition to rules that make homeless encampments illegal in certain areas and her stance against budget proposals that would have sent more money to the Los Angeles Police Department.

“Those are positions she now fully owns as she tries to flip-flop and convince voters otherwise,” Ms. Bass’s campaign spokesman, Alex Stack, said in a statement.

Ms. Raman said she has been a Democrat her whole life, and joined the D.S.A.’s Los Angeles chapter in 2019 because it was “one of the few organizations treating housing affordability with the urgency it demands.”

Since Ms. Raman’s election six years ago, several other D.S.A. members have also been elected to the City Council. A bloc of four members has advanced the group’s policy priorities, including increasing protections for renters and a raise in the minimum wage for some workers.

In recent years, though, Ms. Raman has sometimes staked out positions that seemed to distance her from the D.S.A. She sought to amend a measure backed by D.S.A. colleagues aimed at funding affordable housing programs through a “mansion tax.” Ms. Raman said that the tax had the unintended effect of slowing the development of new, desperately needed apartments. Members of the D.S.A. felt she was caving to developers.

Ms. Raman also clashed with the organization on the Israeli-Palestinian issue, at one point criticizing a D.S.A. statement about the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks.

In this year’s primary race, the D.S.A. chapter opted against formally endorsing Ms. Raman, though it recommended that voters choose her over Ms. Bass and the former reality TV star Spencer Pratt, who ran as a Republican.

“Our endorsement should be earned through a consistent track record of collaboration on working-class issues, not rewarded based on ideological proximity,” members of the D.S.A.’s Los Angeles chapter wrote in an opinion piece for Geese magazine, which describes itself as “a review of American Communism.”

In 2022, Ms. Raman backed Ms. Bass in her run for mayor.

Ms. Bass, a longtime legislator who was on Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s vice-presidential shortlist, ran on what was widely considered a progressive platform, which included strategies for reducing homelessness without incarcerating people. Her opponent was Rick Caruso, a billionaire real estate developer.

This year, Ms. Raman surprised many political observers by jumping into the mayoral race just minutes before the deadline and breaking with Ms. Bass by promising to make the city’s government work better and more efficiently.
